1	# newsetup
2	
3	Scaffold projects from **templates**. A template bundles always-on root files
4	(`config/`) plus any number of optional **modules** (each its own folder), where
5	a module can run shell commands (e.g. `create-next-app`, `django-admin
6	startproject`) and/or drop in files.
7	
8	```
9	newsetup list                                                    # show templates + their modules + parts
10	newsetup new --path . --template default                         # all modules + config here
11	newsetup new --path myapp --template default --modules frontend  # one module (+ config) into ./myapp
12	newsetup new --path myapp --template default --modules frontend backend
13	newsetup new --path . --template default --modules infra            # all infra parts
14	newsetup new --path . --template default --modules infra --only rds # just the RDS part (+ its deps)
15	newsetup new --path . --template default --bare                  # config root files only, no modules
16	newsetup new --path . --template default --bare --force          # overwrite existing root files (no prompt)
17	```
18	
19	## Model
20	
21	- **`--template`** is required — you always state what you're scaffolding. See
22	  `newsetup list` for available names.
23	- **`--path`** is required — no implicit current-directory default. Use `.` for
24	  here, a name for `./<name>`, or a full path. The folder is created if missing.
25	- **`config/`** = always-on. Everything in a template's `config/` folder is
26	  copied to the project **root** on every scaffold (e.g. `CLAUDE.md`). It is not
27	  a selectable module.
28	- **Modules** = every other folder in the template (and/or every section in
29	  `template.toml`). Drop a new folder like `infra/` into a template and it
30	  becomes a module automatically — it shows in `list` and is selectable with
31	  `--only infra`. No code change needed.
32	- **`--modules A B`** builds exactly modules A and B; config still rides along.
33	  Omit `--modules` to build all modules.
34	- **`--only x y`** selects **parts within a single module** — legal only when
35	  exactly one module is selected (via `--modules`) and that module declares
36	  `parts` in `template.toml`. For example `--modules infra --only rds` builds
37	  just the RDS part. Parts auto-pull their dependencies (selecting `ecs` also
38	  pulls `ecr`, `iam`, `rds`, `oidc`), and each part ships its own `*.tf`,
39	  variables, outputs, and a `terraform.tfvars.example` fragment that is
40	  concatenated into one root example. Omit `--only` to build all of a module's
41	  parts.
42	- **`--bare`** builds config root files only (no modules). `--bare` cannot be
43	  combined with `--modules` or `--only`.
44	- **Config conflicts.** If a root config file (e.g. `CLAUDE.md`) already exists,
45	  `newsetup` prompts per file: **[o]verride** (replace), **[m]erge** (keep the
46	  existing file, append a blank line, then the template's content), or
47	  **[s]kip** (leave it untouched). In a non-interactive shell it aborts instead
48	  of prompting — pass `--force` there.
49	- **`--force`** overwrites existing root config files without prompting. Module
50	  folders that already exist and are non-empty always abort (never clobbered).
51	- `git init` runs on every scaffold. If any command exits nonzero, `newsetup`
52	  stops.
53	
54	### Requires on PATH
55	
56	`git`, plus whatever a selected module's commands call — `npx` (Node) for
57	`frontend`, `django-admin` for `backend`. These run as subprocesses via your
58	system PATH; `newsetup` does not install them.
59	
60	## Templates
61	
62	```
63	new_setup/templates/<name>/
64	├── template.toml     # description + per-module { cwd, commands }
65	├── config/           # → copied to project ROOT (always)
66	│   ├── CLAUDE.md
67	│   └── README.md     # empty stub
68	├── backend/          # module "backend": files overlaid into ./backend/
69	│   ├── .gitignore
70	│   ├── CLAUDE.md
71	│   ├── Dockerfile
72	│   ├── entrypoint.sh
73	│   └── migration/{seed,backfill}/   # empty (.gitkeep) seed/backfill dirs
74	├── frontend/         # (optional) overlay files for ./frontend/
75	├── data/             # module "data": empty folder (.gitkeep)
76	├── legacy/           # module "legacy": empty folder (.gitkeep)
77	└── infra/            # module "infra": Terraform, split into PARTS
78	    ├── _core/        #   always copied: main.tf (provider), variables.tf, .gitignore, tfvars fragment
79	    ├── ecr/          #   part "ecr":  ecr.tf  + outputs
80	    ├── rds/          #   part "rds":  database.tf + variables + outputs + tfvars fragment
81	    ├── s3/           #   part "s3":   storage.tf + outputs
82	    ├── iam/          #   part "iam":  ECS execution + infrastructure roles + outputs
83	    ├── ecs/          #   part "ecs":  ecs.tf + variables + outputs + tfvars fragment
84	    └── oidc/         #   part "oidc": github_oidc.tf + variables + outputs + tfvars fragment
85	```
86	
87	`data` and `legacy` are pure file-copy modules that ship an empty folder (a
88	`.gitkeep` so the directory survives in git) — placeholders you fill in per
89	project. `backend` runs `django-admin startproject` and then overlays its
90	Docker + `migration/` scaffold on top.
91	
92	`infra` is a **part-aware** module: instead of one flat folder it has `_core/`
93	(always copied) plus one subfolder per part. `--only <parts>` copies `_core` +
94	the selected parts (and their dependencies) flat into `./infra/`, and every
95	selected part's `*.tfvars.fragment` is concatenated into a single
96	`./infra/terraform.tfvars.example`. Terraform auto-merges all `*.tf` in the
97	folder, so a part only ever contributes the variables/outputs for resources it
98	actually creates. Parts declare dependencies in `template.toml` (`ecs` →
99	`ecr, iam, rds, oidc`; `oidc` → `ecr, ecs`).
100	
101	`template.toml`:
102	
103	```toml
104	description = "Next.js frontend + Django backend + AWS infra (Terraform)"
105	
106	[frontend]
107	cwd = "."                                              # run at root; the command makes ./frontend
108	commands = ["npx create-next-app@latest frontend --yes"]
109	
110	[backend]
111	cwd = "backend"                                        # newsetup makes ./backend, runs the command inside
112	commands = ["django-admin startproject config ."]
113	
114	[infra]                                                # part-aware module (no commands)
115	parts = ["ecr", "rds", "s3", "iam", "ecs", "oidc"]
116	
117	[infra.requires]                                       # auto-pulled deps when a part is selected

# newsetup

Scaffold projects from **templates**. A template bundles always-on root files
(`config/`) plus any number of optional **modules** (each its own folder), where
a module can run shell commands (e.g. `create-next-app`, `django-admin
startproject`) and/or drop in files.

```
newsetup list                                                    # show templates + their modules + parts
newsetup new --path . --template default                         # all modules + config here
newsetup new --path myapp --template default --modules frontend  # one module (+ config) into ./myapp
newsetup new --path myapp --template default --modules frontend backend
newsetup new --path . --template default --modules infra            # all infra parts
newsetup new --path . --template default --modules infra --only rds # just the RDS part (+ its deps)
newsetup new --path . --template default --bare                  # config root files only, no modules
newsetup new --path . --template default --bare --force          # overwrite existing root files (no prompt)
```

## Model

- **`--template`** is required — you always state what you're scaffolding. See
  `newsetup list` for available names.
- **`--path`** is required — no implicit current-directory default. Use `.` for
  here, a name for `./<name>`, or a full path. The folder is created if missing.
- **`config/`** = always-on. Everything in a template's `config/` folder is
  copied to the project **root** on every scaffold (e.g. `CLAUDE.md`). It is not
  a selectable module.
- **Modules** = every other folder in the template (and/or every section in
  `template.toml`). Drop a new folder like `infra/` into a template and it
  becomes a module automatically — it shows in `list` and is selectable with
  `--only infra`. No code change needed.
- **`--modules A B`** builds exactly modules A and B; config still rides along.
  Omit `--modules` to build all modules.
- **`--only x y`** selects **parts within a single module** — legal only when
  exactly one module is selected (via `--modules`) and that module declares
  `parts` in `template.toml`. For example `--modules infra --only rds` builds
  just the RDS part. Parts auto-pull their dependencies (selecting `ecs` also
  pulls `ecr`, `iam`, `rds`, `oidc`), and each part ships its own `*.tf`,
  variables, outputs, and a `terraform.tfvars.example` fragment that is
  concatenated into one root example. Omit `--only` to build all of a module's
  parts.
- **`--bare`** builds config root files only (no modules). `--bare` cannot be
  combined with `--modules` or `--only`.
- **Config conflicts.** If a root config file (e.g. `CLAUDE.md`) already exists,
  `newsetup` prompts per file: **[o]verride** (replace), **[m]erge** (keep the
  existing file, append a blank line, then the template's content), or
  **[s]kip** (leave it untouched). In a non-interactive shell it aborts instead
  of prompting — pass `--force` there.
- **`--force`** overwrites existing root config files without prompting. Module
  folders that already exist and are non-empty always abort (never clobbered).
- `git init` runs on every scaffold. If any command exits nonzero, `newsetup`
  stops.

### Requires on PATH

`git`, plus whatever a selected module's commands call — `npx` (Node) for
`frontend`, `django-admin` for `backend`. These run as subprocesses via your
system PATH; `newsetup` does not install them.

## Templates

```
new_setup/templates/<name>/
├── template.toml     # description + per-module { cwd, commands }
├── config/           # → copied to project ROOT (always)
│   ├── CLAUDE.md
│   └── README.md     # empty stub
├── backend/          # module "backend": files overlaid into ./backend/
│   ├── .gitignore
│   ├── CLAUDE.md
│   ├── Dockerfile
│   ├── entrypoint.sh
│   └── migration/{seed,backfill}/   # empty (.gitkeep) seed/backfill dirs
├── frontend/         # (optional) overlay files for ./frontend/
├── data/             # module "data": empty folder (.gitkeep)
├── legacy/           # module "legacy": empty folder (.gitkeep)
└── infra/            # module "infra": Terraform, split into PARTS
    ├── _core/        #   always copied: main.tf (provider), variables.tf, .gitignore, tfvars fragment
    ├── ecr/          #   part "ecr":  ecr.tf  + outputs
    ├── rds/          #   part "rds":  database.tf + variables + outputs + tfvars fragment
    ├── s3/           #   part "s3":   storage.tf + outputs
    ├── iam/          #   part "iam":  ECS execution + infrastructure roles + outputs
    ├── ecs/          #   part "ecs":  ecs.tf + variables + outputs + tfvars fragment
    └── oidc/         #   part "oidc": github_oidc.tf + variables + outputs + tfvars fragment
```

`data` and `legacy` are pure file-copy modules that ship an empty folder (a
`.gitkeep` so the directory survives in git) — placeholders you fill in per
project. `backend` runs `django-admin startproject` and then overlays its
Docker + `migration/` scaffold on top.

`infra` is a **part-aware** module: instead of one flat folder it has `_core/`
(always copied) plus one subfolder per part. `--only <parts>` copies `_core` +
the selected parts (and their dependencies) flat into `./infra/`, and every
selected part's `*.tfvars.fragment` is concatenated into a single
`./infra/terraform.tfvars.example`. Terraform auto-merges all `*.tf` in the
folder, so a part only ever contributes the variables/outputs for resources it
actually creates. Parts declare dependencies in `template.toml` (`ecs` →
`ecr, iam, rds, oidc`; `oidc` → `ecr, ecs`).

`template.toml`:

```toml
description = "Next.js frontend + Django backend + AWS infra (Terraform)"

[frontend]
cwd = "."                                              # run at root; the command makes ./frontend
commands = ["npx create-next-app@latest frontend --yes"]

[backend]
cwd = "backend"                                        # newsetup makes ./backend, runs the command inside
commands = ["django-admin startproject config ."]

[infra]                                                # part-aware module (no commands)
parts = ["ecr", "rds", "s3", "iam", "ecs", "oidc"]

[infra.requires]                                       # auto-pulled deps when a part is selected
ecs  = ["ecr", "iam", "rds", "oidc"]
oidc = ["ecr", "ecs", "iam"]
```

- A module's `commands` run in `cwd` (relative to the project root; default
  `"."`). `newsetup` creates `cwd` first if it isn't `"."`.
- A module's folder contents (if any) are copied into `./<module>/` after its
  commands run.
- A module with no `template.toml` section is pure file-copy (no commands).
- A module that declares `parts` is part-aware: it copies `_core/` + the
  selected part subfolders (flat), resolves `requires`, and assembles its
  `terraform.tfvars.example` from the parts' `*.tfvars.fragment` files. Part-aware
  modules ignore `cwd`/`commands`.

Templates ship inside the package and are read at runtime via the installed
package's own files — no dependency on this source folder's location.

**Add a template:** create a new folder under `new_setup/templates/`, then
reinstall.

## Install

Installed as a **uv tool** — uv builds it into an isolated environment and puts a
`newsetup` shim on your PATH (`~/.local/bin`). Snapshot install: code + templates
are copied into uv's data dir, so you can move/rename/delete this folder
afterward without breaking the command.

```sh
# from clis/new_setup/
uv tool install .
```

If `newsetup` isn't found, ensure uv's bin dir is on PATH:

```sh
uv tool update-shell   # then restart the shell
```

## Update

Snapshot install — edits here (code or templates) don't affect the installed
command until you reinstall:

```sh
# from clis/new_setup/, after editing
uv tool install --reinstall .
```

## Uninstall

```sh
uv tool uninstall newsetup
```

## MISSING

Known gaps not yet shipped. The planned `infra` module will ship the RDS box
with financexpo's permissive networking default (`publicly_accessible = true`,
open to `0.0.0.0/0`). That still needs hardening before it's a safe default:

6. The security question — this is the important one

> "I thought without the password it was impossible to access these?"

A password is authentication, not network reachability — they're different
layers, and the financexpo config gets the network layer wrong:

```hcl
publicly_accessible = true
cidr_blocks         = ["0.0.0.0/0"]   # port 5432 open to the entire internet
```

That puts Postgres on the public internet. The password only kicks in after an
attacker has already reached the door and is knocking. So you're exposed to
everything that happens before auth:

- Credential brute-force / spray — bots scan 0.0.0.0/0:5432 constantly; a weak
  or leaked password is then an instant breach.
- Pre-auth CVEs — any Postgres vulnerability reachable before login (they exist)
  hits you directly.
- Info leak — the server advertises its version/existence to the whole internet.

Think "a locked door on a public sidewalk" vs "a locked door inside a gated
building." Same lock; very different risk.

The simple standard: keep the database off the public internet. The app reaches
it privately; nothing on the internet can even open a socket to it. Concretely,
the template default becomes:

```hcl
publicly_accessible = false
# ingress: only the app's security group can reach Postgres — not the world
ingress {
  from_port       = 5432
  to_port         = 5432
  protocol        = "tcp"
  security_groups = [aws_security_group.app.id]   # was: cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
}
```

(If ecs isn't selected, there's no app SG, so it falls back to
var.db_allowed_cidr defaulting to the VPC CIDR — still private, never 0.0.0.0/0.)

And I'll keep a warning comment showing the escape hatch for when you genuinely
need to connect from your laptop — scope it to your IP, never the world:

```hcl
# To connect from your machine temporarily, add an ingress rule for YOUR ip only:
#   cidr_blocks = ["<your-ip>/32"]   # never 0.0.0.0/0
# Better: reach it through SSM port-forwarding / a bastion and keep this false.
```

Strong db_password still required — that's defense-in-depth on top, not instead
of. Net effect: secure-by-default, but you can still get in when you need to.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   This session continued development of the `newsetup` CLI's `infra` Terraform module (a uv-tool project scaffolder at `C:\Francisco\github-repositories\mcp_servers\clis\new_setup\`). The overarching intent was to **refactor IAM organization in the generalist `infra` template** based on the user's own synthesized mental model. The user explicitly steered the design through several decisions:
   - Reject the assistant's earlier `_grants/` intersection-folder + `oidc/` proposal.
   - Adopt **Pattern B**: a folder of "general roles" that are inert until a policy attaches, plus per-part permission policies that "light up" those general roles, plus part-local roles that are inseparable from their policy.
   - Name the general-roles folder **`iam`** (rejecting `_iam`, `general-roles`, etc.).
   - Make `iam/` **always-on** (copied every scaffold, like `_core`, not selectable via `--only`).
   - **Ignore the ECS task role for now** (deferred — sidesteps the unverified ECS-Express-task-role question).
   - The user emphasized this is "a generalist template" not a financexpo copy.
   - The user repeatedly required DESIGN DISCUSSION and explicit confirmation BEFORE coding ("show me what you will do", "tell me first before writing anything"). Coding was authorized only with "ok do this ultrathink".

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **newsetup parts engine:** A module declaring `parts` in template.toml is "part-aware": copies `_core/` (always) + `always` folders (always) + selected part subfolders flat into the target, resolves `[module.requires]` dependencies via fixpoint, concatenates each copied folder's `*.tfvars.fragment` into one `terraform.tfvars.example`.
   - **Two-level CLI selection:** `--modules` (which top-level modules) + `--only` (which parts within ONE part-aware module).
   - **`always` parts (NEW this session):** template.toml `always = ["iam"]` declares folders copied on every scaffold regardless of `--only`, not selectable.
   - **IAM role vs policy distinction:** Trust policy (`assume_role_policy`) = "who may assume me" — mandatory, inseparable from the role, stays with the role. Permission policies (inline/attached) = "what I may touch" — separable, distributed to the resource being touched.
   - **Pattern B (chosen + built):** General roles (inert until granted) in always-on `iam/`; per-part permission policies in each resource part; part-local inseparable roles inside the part.
   - **Three ECS Express roles:** execution role + infrastructure role (both inseparable, AWS-managed policy, ECS-only → live in `ecs/iam.tf`); task role (deferred/ignored).
   - **GitHub OIDC deploy role:** general role in `iam/`; its push grant lives in `ecr/`, redeploy grant in `ecs/`; s3/rds contribute no grants (CI never touches them).
   - **Terraform:** all `*.tf` in a directory auto-merge into one module, so cross-file references (a grant in ecr/ referencing a role in iam/) resolve after flat copy. `terraform validate` fails on references to undeclared resources (the dangling-reference constraint that forced the always-on-role design).
   - uv tool snapshot install: `uv tool install --reinstall .` after edits.

3. Files and Code Sections:

   - **infra/iam/iam.tf** (REPLACED — was the ECS exec/infra roles; now the general OIDC deploy role):

     // (ecr, ecs, ...) attaches a permission policy to it. The role's TRUST policy
     // ("who may assume it") lives here because it's inseparable from the role; the
     // PERMISSION policies ("what it may touch") live in each resource's part.

     // GitHub Actions OIDC trust + deploy role for your deploy workflow.
     resource "aws_iam_openid_connect_provider" "github_actions" {
       url            = "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
       client_id_list = ["sts.amazonaws.com"]
       thumbprint_list = [

         "1c58a3a8518e8759bf075b76b750d4f2df264fcd",
       ]
     }
     data "aws_iam_policy_document" "github_actions_assume" {
       statement {
         effect  = "Allow"
         actions = ["sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity"]
         principals {
           type        = "Federated"
           identifiers = [aws_iam_openid_connect_provider.github_actions.arn]
         }
         condition { test = "StringEquals"; variable = "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud"; values = ["sts.amazonaws.com"] }
         condition { test = "StringEquals"; variable = "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub"; values = ["repo:${var.github_repo}:ref:refs/heads/master"] }
       }

       assume_role_policy = data.aws_iam_policy_document.github_actions_assume.json

# newsetup

Scaffold projects from **templates**. A template bundles always-on root files
(`config/`) plus any number of optional **modules** (each its own folder), where
a module can run shell commands (e.g. `create-next-app`, `django-admin
startproject`) and/or drop in files.

```
newsetup list                                                    # show templates + their modules + parts
newsetup new --path . --template default                         # all modules + config here
newsetup new --path myapp --template default --modules frontend  # one module (+ config) into ./myapp
newsetup new --path myapp --template default --modules frontend backend
newsetup new --path . --template default --modules infra            # all infra parts
newsetup new --path . --template default --modules infra --only rds # just the RDS part (+ its deps)
newsetup new --path . --template default --bare                  # config root files only, no modules
newsetup new --path . --template default --bare --force          # overwrite existing root files (no prompt)
```

## Model

- **`--template`** is required — you always state what you're scaffolding. See
  `newsetup list` for available names.
- **`--path`** is required — no implicit current-directory default. Use `.` for
  here, a name for `./<name>`, or a full path. The folder is created if missing.
- **`config/`** = always-on. Everything in a template's `config/` folder is
  copied to the project **root** on every scaffold (e.g. `CLAUDE.md`). It is not
  a selectable module.
- **Modules** = every other folder in the template (and/or every section in
  `template.toml`). Drop a new folder like `infra/` into a template and it
  becomes a module automatically — it shows in `list` and is selectable with
  `--only infra`. No code change needed.
- **`--modules A B`** builds exactly modules A and B; config still rides along.
  Omit `--modules` to build all modules.
- **`--only x y`** selects **parts within a single module** — legal only when
  exactly one module is selected (via `--modules`) and that module declares
  `parts` in `template.toml`. For example `--modules infra --only rds` builds
  just the RDS part. Parts auto-pull their dependencies (selecting `ecs` also
  pulls `ecr`, `rds`), and each part ships its own `*.tf`, variables, outputs,
  and a `terraform.tfvars.example` fragment that is concatenated into one root
  example. A module can also declare `always` parts (e.g. infra's `iam`) that
  are copied on every scaffold regardless of `--only`. Omit `--only` to build
  all of a module's selectable parts.
- **`--bare`** builds config root files only (no modules). `--bare` cannot be
  combined with `--modules` or `--only`.
- **Config conflicts.** If a root config file (e.g. `CLAUDE.md`) already exists,
  `newsetup` prompts per file: **[o]verride** (replace), **[m]erge** (keep the
  existing file, append a blank line, then the template's content), or
  **[s]kip** (leave it untouched). In a non-interactive shell it aborts instead
  of prompting — pass `--force` there.
- **`--force`** overwrites existing root config files without prompting. Module
  folders that already exist and are non-empty always abort (never clobbered).
- `git init` runs on every scaffold. If any command exits nonzero, `newsetup`
  stops.

### Requires on PATH

`git`, plus whatever a selected module's commands call — `npx` (Node) for
`frontend`, `django-admin` for `backend`. These run as subprocesses via your
system PATH; `newsetup` does not install them.

## Templates

```
new_setup/templates/<name>/
├── template.toml     # description + per-module { cwd, commands }
├── config/           # → copied to project ROOT (always)
│   ├── CLAUDE.md
│   └── README.md     # empty stub
├── backend/          # module "backend": files overlaid into ./backend/
│   ├── .gitignore
│   ├── CLAUDE.md
│   ├── Dockerfile
│   ├── entrypoint.sh
│   └── migration/{seed,backfill}/   # empty (.gitkeep) seed/backfill dirs
├── frontend/         # (optional) overlay files for ./frontend/
├── data/             # module "data": empty folder (.gitkeep)
├── legacy/           # module "legacy": empty folder (.gitkeep)
└── infra/            # module "infra": Terraform, split into PARTS
    ├── _core/        #   always copied: main.tf (provider), variables.tf, .gitignore, tfvars fragment
    ├── iam/          #   always copied: general roles (GitHub OIDC provider + deploy role) — inert until a part grants it
    ├── ecr/          #   part "ecr":  ecr.tf + deploy_policy.tf (push grant) + outputs
    ├── rds/          #   part "rds":  database.tf + variables + outputs + tfvars fragment
    ├── s3/           #   part "s3":   storage.tf + outputs
    └── ecs/          #   part "ecs":  ecs.tf + iam.tf (execution/infra roles) + deploy_policy.tf (redeploy grant) + variables + outputs + tfvars fragment
```

`data` and `legacy` are pure file-copy modules that ship an empty folder (a
`.gitkeep` so the directory survives in git) — placeholders you fill in per
project. `backend` runs `django-admin startproject` and then overlays its
Docker + `migration/` scaffold on top.

`infra` is a **part-aware** module: instead of one flat folder it has `_core/`
plus `iam/` (both **always copied**) plus one subfolder per selectable part.
`--only <parts>` copies `_core` + `iam` + the selected parts (and their
dependencies) flat into `./infra/`, and every copied folder's
`*.tfvars.fragment` is concatenated into a single
`./infra/terraform.tfvars.example`. Terraform auto-merges all `*.tf` in the
folder, so a part only ever contributes the variables/outputs for resources it
actually creates. Parts declare dependencies in `template.toml` (`ecs` →
`ecr, rds`).

**IAM is split by what a role *is*.** General roles that do nothing until a
policy is attached (the GitHub Actions deploy role + its OIDC provider) live in
the always-on `iam/` layer — declared once, inert by default. Each resource part
then ships the *permission* that lights that role up for itself: `ecr/` grants
image push, `ecs/` grants service redeploy; `s3`/`rds` grant nothing (CI never
touches them). Roles that are inseparable from their policy and meaningless
without their resource (the ECS task-execution + Express infrastructure roles)
live inside the part itself (`ecs/iam.tf`). The role's *trust* policy ("who may
assume it") always rides with the role; only *permission* policies move out to
the parts.

`template.toml`:

```toml
description = "Next.js frontend + Django backend + AWS infra (Terraform)"

[frontend]
cwd = "."                                              # run at root; the command makes ./frontend
commands = ["npx create-next-app@latest frontend --yes"]

[backend]
cwd = "backend"                                        # newsetup makes ./backend, runs the command inside
commands = ["django-admin startproject config ."]

[infra]                                                # part-aware module (no commands)
parts  = ["ecr", "rds", "s3", "ecs"]                   # selectable with --only
always = ["iam"]                                       # copied every scaffold, like _core; not selectable

[infra.requires]                                       # auto-pulled deps when a part is selected
ecs = ["ecr", "rds"]
```

- A module's `commands` run in `cwd` (relative to the project root; default
  `"."`). `newsetup` creates `cwd` first if it isn't `"."`.
- A module's folder contents (if any) are copied into `./<module>/` after its
  commands run.
- A module with no `template.toml` section is pure file-copy (no commands).
- A module that declares `parts` is part-aware: it copies `_core/` + any
  `always` subfolders + the selected part subfolders (flat), resolves
  `requires`, and assembles its `terraform.tfvars.example` from the copied
  folders' `*.tfvars.fragment` files. Part-aware modules ignore `cwd`/`commands`.

Templates ship inside the package and are read at runtime via the installed
package's own files — no dependency on this source folder's location.

**Add a template:** create a new folder under `new_setup/templates/`, then
reinstall.

## Install

Installed as a **uv tool** — uv builds it into an isolated environment and puts a
`newsetup` shim on your PATH (`~/.local/bin`). Snapshot install: code + templates
are copied into uv's data dir, so you can move/rename/delete this folder
afterward without breaking the command.

```sh
# from clis/new_setup/
uv tool install .
```

If `newsetup` isn't found, ensure uv's bin dir is on PATH:

```sh
uv tool update-shell   # then restart the shell
```

## Update

Snapshot install — edits here (code or templates) don't affect the installed
command until you reinstall:

```sh
# from clis/new_setup/, after editing
uv tool install --reinstall .
```

## Uninstall

```sh
uv tool uninstall newsetup
```

## MISSING

Known gaps not yet shipped. The planned `infra` module will ship the RDS box
with financexpo's permissive networking default (`publicly_accessible = true`,
open to `0.0.0.0/0`). That still needs hardening before it's a safe default:

6. The security question — this is the important one

> "I thought without the password it was impossible to access these?"

A password is authentication, not network reachability — they're different
layers, and the financexpo config gets the network layer wrong:

```hcl
publicly_accessible = true
cidr_blocks         = ["0.0.0.0/0"]   # port 5432 open to the entire internet
```

That puts Postgres on the public internet. The password only kicks in after an
attacker has already reached the door and is knocking. So you're exposed to
everything that happens before auth:

- Credential brute-force / spray — bots scan 0.0.0.0/0:5432 constantly; a weak
  or leaked password is then an instant breach.
- Pre-auth CVEs — any Postgres vulnerability reachable before login (they exist)
  hits you directly.
- Info leak — the server advertises its version/existence to the whole internet.

Think "a locked door on a public sidewalk" vs "a locked door inside a gated
building." Same lock; very different risk.

The simple standard: keep the database off the public internet. The app reaches
it privately; nothing on the internet can even open a socket to it. Concretely,
the template default becomes:

```hcl
publicly_accessible = false
# ingress: only the app's security group can reach Postgres — not the world
ingress {
  from_port       = 5432
  to_port         = 5432
  protocol        = "tcp"
  security_groups = [aws_security_group.app.id]   # was: cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
}
```

(If ecs isn't selected, there's no app SG, so it falls back to
var.db_allowed_cidr defaulting to the VPC CIDR — still private, never 0.0.0.0/0.)

And I'll keep a warning comment showing the escape hatch for when you genuinely
need to connect from your laptop — scope it to your IP, never the world:

```hcl
# To connect from your machine temporarily, add an ingress rule for YOUR ip only:
#   cidr_blocks = ["<your-ip>/32"]   # never 0.0.0.0/0
# Better: reach it through SSM port-forwarding / a bastion and keep this false.
```

Strong db_password still required — that's defense-in-depth on top, not instead
of. Net effect: secure-by-default, but you can still get in when you need to.

        Export and import all your sessions so nothing is missed. You can:
        - Export sessions with detailed summaries
        - List your own sessions
        - Browse sessions shared with your teams
        - Import sessions from teammates
        - Search sessions by repository

        - Use proper HTML structure with <!DOCTYPE html>, <html>, <head>, and <body> tags
        - Use semantic HTML5 tags: <header>, <main>, <section>, <article>, <footer>
        - Use heading tags (<h1>, <h2>, <h3>, etc.) for document structure
        - Use <pre><code> blocks for code snippets, with class attribute for syntax highlighting (e.g., <code class="language-python">)
        - Use <ul>/<ol> and <li> for lists
        - Use <strong> and <em> for emphasis
        - Use <a href="url"> for links
        - Include proper CSS styling in <style> tags or inline for better presentation

content.text:
Now I can explain it concretely against what's actually in the files.

## How it works *right now*

Look at `ecs/ecs.tf` line 21 — this is the whole story:

```hcl
environment {
  name  = "PROD_DATABASE_URL"
  value = "postgres://${var.db_username}:${var.db_password}@${aws_db_instance.postgres.endpoint}/...?sslmode=require"
                                                            ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
}
```

That `aws_db_instance.postgres.endpoint` is a **live resource reference** — ecs is reaching directly into the rds part and reading an attribute off the actual database resource. This is the "direct reference / auto-wires in one apply" model.

Consequences of this being how it is today:

- **ecs literally cannot stand alone.** If you `--only ecs`, Terraform sees `aws_db_instance.postgres` referenced but never declared → `terraform validate` fails with a dangling reference. That's *exactly why* `template.toml` has `ecs = ["ecr", "rds"]` in `[infra.requires]` — selecting ecs is forced to drag rds in, because the code won't even parse otherwise.
- **The upside:** when both are present, it's magic. One `terraform apply` creates the RDS box, Terraform notices ecs depends on `aws_db_instance.postgres.endpoint`, builds rds *first*, then injects the real endpoint into the ECS env var automatically. Zero manual steps. The DB URL is always correct because it's computed from the live resource.

So today: **ecs and rds are welded together.** "ecs" really means "ecs+rds, always."

## What "the wiring is a variable" means

The decoupled alternative replaces that live reference with a plain input variable:

```hcl
# instead of referencing aws_db_instance.postgres.endpoint:
value = var.database_url   # a string you pass in, default ""
```

Now ecs no longer mentions any rds resource. It just wants *a string*. Where that string comes from is none of ecs's business — could be RDS, Supabase, Neon, anything.

"The wiring is a variable, not a live resource reference" = **the connection between the two parts is now a value you type in, instead of a link Terraform follows automatically.**

That buys independence but costs you the auto-magic. Compare the two worlds when you want **both** ecs and rds:

| | Live reference (today) | Variable (decoupled) |
|---|---|---|
| `--only ecs` alone | ❌ won't validate | ✅ runs, no DB |
| ecs + rds together | one `apply`, auto-wired | **two-step apply** |

The "two-step apply" is the honest tax. Because `var.database_url` needs a value *before* apply, but the real endpoint doesn't exist *until* rds is applied, you can't do it in one shot:

1. `terraform apply` → rds comes up. Read its endpoint: `terraform output -raw rds_endpoint` (that output already exists in `rds/outputs_rds.tf`).
2. Paste it into `database_url` in your tfvars, `terraform apply` again → ecs picks it up.

With the live reference, Terraform's dependency graph does that ordering for you in a single apply. With a variable, *you* are the dependency graph.

## The trade-off in one sentence

- **Live reference** = one-apply convenience, but ecs is permanently chained to rds (no "ecs alone").
- **Variable** = ecs works with any database (the actual meaning of "generalist"), but combining ecs+rds becomes a manual two-step.

For a generalist template the variable wins, because the template's job is to scaffold *any* project, not to assume every project pairs ECS with an RDS box in the same stack. The convenience you lose is recoverable any time — a project that's *always* ecs+rds can drop the one-line live reference back in.

One more consequence worth flagging, since it reverses something said earlier: decoupling flips the dependency direction. Today `ecs → rds` (ecs needs rds to exist). Decoupled, ecs needs *nothing* — so `[infra.requires]` would lose the `ecs = ["ecr", "rds"]` rds entry (ecr stays, since the image reference `aws_ecr_repository.backend` is still a live reference). ecs would then pull only ecr.

Want me to actually make this change, or were you just mapping the terrain first?

content.text:
Let me challenge the premise directly, because I think the framing is slightly off in a way that dissolves the problem.

## First: who actually needs that env? Not ECS. Not RDS. The *app*.

`PROD_DATABASE_URL` isn't there because ECS needs it or because AWS requires it. ECS doesn't care — it'll run a container with zero env vars all day. RDS doesn't care either; it just sits there listening on 5432.

That env exists because **Django needs to know where its database is.** It's application config. ECS is just the delivery truck that hands the app its environment at boot.

That reframe matters, because it tells you who *owns* the env: the application — and the application is what ecs deploys. So the DB url conceptually belongs **with ecs**, not with rds. rds isn't the owner of that wiring; rds is merely one possible *supplier of the value*.

## Why your grant analogy inverts here

You're pattern-matching to the IAM refactor we just did: "the grant lives in the part, lighting up the shared thing." That worked for IAM for a specific reason — and that reason is exactly what's missing here.

- **IAM grant (ecr → role):** ecr genuinely *owns* the permission. "I am the ECR repo, and I permit pushes to me." The grant is a fact about ecr. It belongs in ecr/. The role is the shared surface; ecr lights it up. Ownership flows **part → shared thing**. ✅
- **DB env (rds → ecs):** rds does *not* own "the app should connect to me." The app owns its need for a database; rds just happens to be able to answer it. Ownership flows the **opposite way** — the consumer (ecs/app) owns the need, rds is a value source.

So "rds contributes the env to ecs, like a grant" is upside-down. It'd be rds reaching into the app's config to declare what the app needs — rds doesn't have that authority or knowledge. The app does.

## And even if you wanted to, Terraform won't let you

Here's the mechanical wall, and it's the real reason the grant pattern can't transfer:

The IAM grant works because `aws_iam_role_policy` is a **separate, independently-addressable resource**. ecr can put it in its own file; flat-copy merges it; it attaches to the role by reference. Separable.

The DB env is a **nested block inside the one `aws_ecs_express_gateway_service` resource**. It is not separable. And Terraform forbids splitting a single resource across files. So rds *cannot* drop a file that injects an `environment { ... }` into a resource declared in ecs/ecs.tf. There's no syntax for it.

You might think "ok, make the env a `dynamic` block over a variable/local, and have rds fill it." That hits two more walls, both fatal:

1. **The value is computed.** The RDS endpoint (`xyz.abc123.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com`) is assigned *by AWS at apply time* — that random hash isn't knowable beforehand. To move a computed attribute from resource A into resource B **in one apply**, Terraform *must* see a live reference A→B in its graph. There is no other mechanism. And a live reference is precisely what makes ecs fail to validate when rds is absent. Computed value ⇒ live reference ⇒ dangles without rds. Unavoidable.

2. **You can't stub-and-override across merged files.** For optional injection you'd want ecs to ship a `local.db_env = {}` default that rds overrides when present. Terraform rejects duplicate local keys — no overrides. And if only rds defines the local, ecs's reference to it dangles when rds is absent. Either way, dead.

So: **at the flat-file-merge level, "rds optionally injects the DB env into ecs" is not buildable.** Not "hard" — structurally impossible, because computed-value-coupling forces a live reference and Terraform offers no override/stub escape. There is no clever HCL that gets you there.

## The only two real escapes (and they're big)

**Escape A — runtime indirection (the *true* grant analog).** Stop putting the URL as a literal env. Instead, ecs's task references a secret by a *conventional name* — a string like `/${project}/${environment}/DATABASE_URL` (SSM Parameter Store / Secrets Manager). A string isn't a Terraform reference, so ecs validates alone. Then rds contributes a **separable** `aws_ssm_parameter` resource (lives in rds/, exactly like ecr's deploy_policy.tf lives in ecr/) that fills that name with the computed endpoint. One apply, no dangling ref, ecs standalone-valid, and *now* it's genuinely symmetric to the IAM grant — because the contributed thing finally is a separable resource. This is the architecturally "right" answer. But: it adds Secrets Manager/SSM as a moving part, needs the task-execution role granted `ssm:GetParameters`, and hinges on `aws_ecs_express_gateway_service` supporting `valueFrom`-style secrets — which is an unverified AWS specific, the same kind of rabbit hole as the task-role question you deliberately deferred. Not a "finish soon" move.

**Escape B — newsetup picks the wiring at scaffold time.** The thing that "adds the env if rds appears" is *newsetup*, not Terraform. Select ecs+rds → emit the live-reference env (today's ecs.tf, one-apply magic). Select ecs alone → emit `var.database_url`. Terraform stays clean in both. Cost: real new complexity in the parts engine (conditional cross-part content) plus two maintained variants. Also not "finish soon."

## My recommendation, given "finish soon" + "I'm coupling them"

You said it yourself: *"I'm coupling them together."* So stop fighting for ecs-standalone. **Make ecs⇒rds the template's contract** — which is *already* exactly what's built: the live reference + `[infra.requires] ecs = ["ecr", "rds"]`. Selecting ecs pulls rds, one apply wires the real endpoint, done. The hardcoded env isn't a wart; it's correct, because in this template ecs never exists without rds.

Then serve "generalist" with **one comment, not machinery** — a couple of commented lines right above that env in ecs/ecs.tf:

```hcl
# Uses the RDS box created in this stack. To point at an external DB
# (Supabase, Neon, RDS in another stack) instead, replace the value with:
#   value = var.database_url   # and drop rds from [infra.requires]
```

That gives the generalist escape hatch (a 30-second manual edit) without building Escape A or B, keeps the one-apply magic you want, and ships today. If you later decide the SSM pattern is worth it, Escape A is the upgrade path — but it's a *next* project, not this one.

Net: the env belongs in ecs because the *app* owns it; rds is just the supplier; the grant pattern can't invert; and the cleanest finish is to embrace the coupling you already said you want and document the one-line generalist swap.

content.text:
Here's the concrete mechanism, traced end to end against the actual engine. The trick that makes it tractable is to **stop the variance from living in `ecs.tf` at all** — collapse it down to a single symbol, then swap only that symbol's definition.

## Step 1: make `ecs.tf` stop varying

Today the variance is buried inside the service resource (the env value), which is unsplittable. So pull it out behind a `local`. `ecs.tf`'s env block becomes stable forever:

```hcl
environment {
  name  = "PROD_DATABASE_URL"
  value = local.database_url     # ← stable. never changes between scenarios.
}
```

Now `ecs.tf` references `local.database_url` and doesn't care where it comes from. All the variance is pushed into the *definition* of that one local — a tiny separate file.

## Step 2: two tiny variant files (one symbol, two definitions)

**Coupled** (the value is the live RDS reference — today's magic):
```hcl
# db_local.when-rds.tf
locals {
  database_url = "postgres://${var.db_username}:${var.db_password}@${aws_db_instance.postgres.endpoint}/...?sslmode=require"
}
```

**Standalone** (the value is an input string — generalist):
```hcl
# db_local.unless-rds.tf
variable "database_url" { type = string, default = "" }
locals {
  database_url = var.database_url
}
```

Exactly **one** of these is allowed to land in `./infra/`, ever. If both landed, Terraform errors on duplicate `local.database_url`. So the whole game reduces to: *newsetup must copy the right one and suppress the other.*

## Step 3: the one engine change — presence-gated filenames

newsetup already knows the resolved part set at copy time (the `parts` list in `copy_parts_module`). Teach it one filename rule:

- `foo.when-<part>.tf` → copy **only if** `<part>` ∈ resolved parts, writing it as `foo.tf`.
- `foo.unless-<part>.tf` → copy **only if** `<part>` ∉ resolved parts, writing it as `foo.tf`.

That's the entire new capability: parse a `.when-X` / `.unless-X` infix, check membership, strip the infix on write. In `copy_parts_module`'s file loop, before `shutil.copy2`, a ~6-line gate.

## Step 4: trace both scaffolds

**`--only ecs`** (resolves to `ecs, ecr, iam, _core` — note rds is *not* pulled, because in this model ecs no longer requires it):
- `db_local.when-rds.tf` → rds absent → **skipped**.
- `db_local.unless-rds.tf` → rds absent → copied as `db_local.tf` → `local.database_url = var.database_url`.
- `ecs.tf` references `local.database_url` ✅. No `aws_db_instance` anywhere ✅. Validates standalone. App points wherever you set `database_url` (Supabase, Neon…).

**`--only ecs rds`** (or full infra):
- `db_local.when-rds.tf` → rds present → copied as `db_local.tf` → live reference to `aws_db_instance.postgres.endpoint`.
- `db_local.unless-rds.tf` → rds present → **skipped**.
- One `apply`: Terraform sees ecs→rds via the local, builds rds first, injects the real endpoint. The magic, intact.

Never both files → never a duplicate-local error. The "thing that adds the wiring when rds appears" is the filename gate.

## Step 5: the honest wrinkle (tfvars + the variable)

Two satellite pieces also have to ride the gate, or they leak:

- The `variable "database_url"` declaration only makes sense standalone — so it lives **inside** `db_local.unless-rds.tf` (shown above). When rds is present, that file is skipped, so the variable simply doesn't exist. Good.
- The tfvars example line. Standalone wants `database_url = "CHANGE_ME"` in `terraform.tfvars.example`; coupled wants *nothing* (the value is computed, not user-supplied). So the fragment must also be gated: a file named `db.unless-rds.tfvars.fragment`. That means the gate parser has to compose with the existing `*.tfvars.fragment` matcher — strip `.unless-rds`, *then* still recognize `.tfvars.fragment`. Doable, but it's the fiddly bit: two filename conventions now interacting.

## The cost, stated plainly

- **New engine surface:** a filename mini-language (`when-`/`unless-`) that has to compose with the existing fragment-suffix logic. It's small (~10 lines) but it's *permanent vocabulary* every future template author must learn and you must document.
- **Two maintained variants** of the DB wiring that must stay in sync (same env semantics, two definitions).
- **It generalizes**, which is the upside — any "this file only when part X is/ isn't present" need is now expressible (not just DB). That's either a feature or a footgun depending on how much conditional cross-part content you actually expect. So far you have exactly *one* case.

## My call (unchanged, now that you can see the machinery)

Building a general conditional-emission sub-language to serve a single env line is a lot of permanent surface for one case — and it buys you "ecs-standalone," which you said you don't even want ("I'm coupling them"). The same outcome you actually care about (one-apply magic when rds is there) is *already shipping* via the live reference + `requires`. The generalist escape is a one-line manual swap documented in a comment.

So: Escape B is real and clean-ish — the `local.database_url` indirection is genuinely the right shape — but I'd only build the filename-gate engine if a *second or third* conditional-content case shows up. For one line, the comment wins. If you want, I'll do the zero-cost half of this anyway: refactor the env to go through `local.database_url` now (pure cleanup, no engine change), so that *if* you ever want Escape B later, the hard part is already done and it's just dropping the two gated files in.

Done — `db_local.empty.tf` it is. Quick note on what that rename implies, then the re-explanation you asked for.

## What the rename changes (small but worth saying)

`unless-rds` encoded the *condition* in the filename. `empty` instead names the file by *what it is* — the inert fallback. So the engine rule shifts slightly:

- `db_local.empty.tf` = the fallback definition of `local.database_url` (= `var.database_url`, inert). Used **when nothing supersedes it.**
- `db_local.when-rds.tf` = the real definition (live RDS reference). Used **when rds is present.**

Both target the same output name, `db_local.tf`. Rule: the `.when-rds` one wins if rds is present; otherwise the `.empty` one fills in. It's an if/else over one output file — arguably cleaner than `unless-rds`, because ecs's fallback file no longer hardcodes the name "rds" in it. ecs just says "here's my empty default"; rds is the one that knows to override.

## The tfvars part, re-explained from scratch

**What `terraform.tfvars.example` is:** newsetup builds one example file by gluing together every copied folder's `*.tfvars.fragment` snippets. It's the "copy this to terraform.tfvars and fill in your real values" starter. Each part contributes the lines for the variables *it* introduces.

**Why the DB line is conditional** — look at what the user actually has to type in each scenario:

- **Empty / standalone:** the DB url comes from `var.database_url`, which the user **must supply**. So the example file *should* contain a prompt line:
  ```hcl
  database_url = "CHANGE_ME"   # postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db
  ```
- **Coupled / rds present:** there is **no** `var.database_url` — the value is computed from the live RDS resource at apply time. The user supplies **nothing**. So the example file must **not** contain a `database_url` line. If it did, it'd be telling the user to set a variable that doesn't exist — broken and confusing.

So that one `database_url = "CHANGE_ME"` line has to appear **only in the empty case** — exactly the same on/off condition as `db_local.empty.tf`. It's a sibling that must ride the same gate.

**Now the "fiddly bit" — why two conventions collide on one file.**

The engine has two *independent* filename rules:

1. **Fragment rule:** "does the name end in `.tfvars.fragment`? → don't copy it as a file; instead append its text into `terraform.tfvars.example`."
2. **Gate rule:** "does the name carry `.empty` / `.when-rds`? → decide whether to include it at all, and strip the marker."

For the DB prompt line, **both rules apply to the same file at once.** Its name has to carry *both* markers:

```
db.empty.tfvars.fragment
   └gate┘ └─fragment suffix─┘
```

So when the engine scans that filename it can't just run one rule — it has to do both, in the right order:

1. First see the gate marker `.empty` → "is the empty variant active? If rds is present, **skip this entirely**."
2. Only if it survives the gate, recognize the remaining `.tfvars.fragment` → "append to the example file."

That's the interaction. The two conventions aren't layered cleanly — they're stacked on one name and have to be parsed together. If you wrote the fragment check naïvely (`if name.endswith(".tfvars.fragment")`) it would happily concat `db.empty.tfvars.fragment` even when rds is present, leaking a `database_url = "CHANGE_ME"` line into a coupled scaffold that has no such variable. So the gate check has to run *first*, and the fragment matcher has to look at the name *after* the gate marker is stripped. One file, two rules, order-dependent — that's all "the fiddly bit" means. It's maybe 4 extra lines, but it's the spot where a careless implementation silently leaks the wrong tfvars line.

This is exactly why, for a *single* DB line, I still lean toward the documented one-line comment over building the gate. But if you want the gate, the `db_local.empty.tf` framing is the right shape and I can wire it cleanly — the ordering trap above is the one thing I'd be careful about.

content.text:
Two real collisions confirmed (the `db_local.tf` entry is a false positive — the gate guarantees only one variant ever emits):

1. **`iam.tf`** — `iam/` (deploy role) vs `ecs/` (exec/infra roles) → ecs clobbers the deploy role.
2. **`deploy_policy.tf`** — `ecr/` (push grant) vs `ecs/` (redeploy grant) → ecs clobbers ecr's push grant *silently* (no validate error, just lost).

Both are from the prior session's IAM refactor, which never ran `validate`. The flat-copy model requires globally-unique filenames; these aren't. Fix = rename to the existing `_<part>` convention (pure renames; Terraform merges all `*.tf` regardless of filename, so the merged module is unchanged):

**IAM is split by what a role *is*.** General roles that do nothing until a
policy is attached (the GitHub Actions deploy role + its OIDC provider) live in
the always-on `iam/` layer — declared once, inert by default. Each resource part
then ships the *permission* that lights that role up for itself: `ecr/` grants
image push, `ecs/` grants service redeploy; `s3`/`rds` grant nothing (CI never
touches them). Roles that are inseparable from their policy and meaningless
without their resource (the ECS task-execution + Express infrastructure roles)
live inside the part itself (`ecs/iam_ecs.tf`). The role's *trust* policy ("who
may assume it") always rides with the role; only *permission* policies move out
to the parts.

**The DB URL is gated on whether `rds` is in the scaffold.** `ecs.tf` always
reads `local.database_url`; what defines that local is chosen at scaffold time
by a filename gate. `db_local.when-rds.tf` builds the URL live from the in-stack
RDS box (`aws_db_instance.postgres.endpoint`) and is emitted only when `rds` is
present — so `ecs` + `rds` is a single `terraform apply`, auto-wired. When `rds`
is absent, `db_local.empty.tf` supplies `local.database_url = var.database_url`
instead, letting `ecs` point at any external database (Supabase, Neon, an RDS in
another stack) and validate standalone. The two files are one logical unit keyed
on the stem `db_local`; exactly one is ever copied, and the matching
`database_url = "CHANGE_ME"` tfvars line appears only in the `var`-driven case.
This is the general **gate convention** any template can use: `foo.when-<part>.*`
is copied only if `<part>` is selected, and `foo.empty.*` is its fallback,
copied only when no active `when-` sibling (same stem) supersedes it. The
`.when-<part>` / `.empty` segment is stripped from the output name.

content.text:
Done. Escape B is implemented, verified, and the docs match.

## What I built

**Engine (`new_setup/cli.py`)**
- `parse_gate(name)` — reads a `.when-<part>` or `.empty` segment out of a filename, returns `(kind, part, base, stem)`.
- `copy_parts_module` rewritten to two passes: pass 1 finds which `(dir, stem)` units have an active `.when-<part>` (part present); pass 2 emits in order — `.when-X` only if X is present, `.empty` only if no active `when-` sibling shares its stem, de-gating *before* the `.tfvars.fragment` check so gated fragments resolve too.
- **Collision guard** — aborts with a "template bug" error if two parts would flatten to the same output name (turns silent overwrite into a loud failure).

**Template**
- `ecs/ecs.tf` env → `local.database_url`.
- `ecs/db_local.when-rds.tf` (live RDS ref) + `ecs/db_local.empty.tf` (`var.database_url`) + `ecs/db_local.empty.tfvars.fragment` (`database_url = "CHANGE_ME"`).
- `template.toml`: `ecs = ["ecr"]` (dropped `rds` so the gate is live).
- Renamed two pre-existing collisions surfaced by the guard: `ecs/iam.tf`→`iam_ecs.tf`, `ecr/deploy_policy.tf`→`deploy_policy_ecr.tf`, `ecs/deploy_policy.tf`→`deploy_policy_ecs.tf`.

## Verified
- `terraform validate` → **Success** on `--only ecs`, `--only ecs rds`, full infra, `--only rds`, `--only s3`.
- Gate resolves right: ecs-alone → `var.database_url` + `CHANGE_ME` tfvars line; ecs+rds → live RDS ref, **no** tfvars line.
- No `.when-`/`.empty`/`.fragment` leaks; tfvars order `core → github_repo → per-part`.
- Collision guard fires on a planted clash; template left clean.

## Two things worth your eye
1. **The requires change is the real behavior shift.** `ecs` no longer drags in `rds`. `--only ecs` now gives a standalone, external-DB service; you opt into the one-apply RDS coupling by adding `rds` to the selection. This is the generalist posture — flag if you'd rather force coupling.
2. **The pre-existing collisions were silently destroying config** (the deploy role and the ECR push grant both vanished in any ecs scaffold). That never validated before because `validate` was never run. It's fixed, and the guard prevents the whole class from recurring.

Two pre-existing items I did **not** touch (still open, per earlier scope): the deferred ECS **task role**, and the permissive **RDS networking** default documented in README MISSING. Nothing here is committed — say the word if you want a commit.

Here's the layout, in two views — the **template source** (what you author) and the **scaffolded output** (what lands in `./infra/`, after the gate rewrites names).

## Template source — `templates/default/infra/`

```
infra/
├── _core/                          # always copied (provider, base vars)
│   ├── main.tf
│   ├── variables.tf
│   ├── .gitignore                  # (dotfile; ignores .tfstate/.tfvars/etc.)
│   └── core.tfvars.fragment
├── iam/                            # always copied (general roles)
│   ├── iam.tf                      #   GitHub OIDC provider + deploy role (inert until granted)
│   ├── variables_iam.tf           #   github_repo
│   ├── outputs_iam.tf             #   github_actions_role_arn
│   └── iam.tfvars.fragment        #   github_repo = "CHANGE_ME"
├── ecr/                            # part "ecr"
│   ├── ecr.tf
│   ├── deploy_policy_ecr.tf       #   ecr slice of the deploy role (push grant)
│   └── outputs_ecr.tf
├── rds/                            # part "rds"
│   ├── database.tf
│   ├── variables_rds.tf           #   db_username, db_password
│   ├── outputs_rds.tf
│   └── rds.tfvars.fragment
├── s3/                             # part "s3"
│   ├── storage.tf
│   └── outputs_s3.tf
└── ecs/                            # part "ecs"
    ├── ecs.tf                      #   service; reads local.database_url
    ├── iam_ecs.tf                  #   execution + Express infra roles (inseparable)
    ├── deploy_policy_ecs.tf        #   ecs slice of the deploy role (redeploy grant)
    ├── db_local.when-rds.tf        #   ┐ GATE: local.database_url =
    ├── db_local.empty.tf           #   ┘   live RDS ref  (when rds present)
    ├── db_local.empty.tfvars.fragment  #     OR var.database_url (when rds absent)
    ├── variables_ecs.tf
    ├── outputs_ecs.tf
    └── ecs.tfvars.fragment
```

The three `db_local.*` files are the gate: same stem `db_local`, exactly one variant survives per scaffold.

## Scaffolded output — flat into `./infra/`

The gate strips `.when-rds` / `.empty` from names, so both variants land as plain `db_local.tf`:

**`--only ecs`** (pulls `ecr`; rds **absent** → empty branch):
```
infra/
├── main.tf  variables.tf  .gitignore        ← _core
├── iam.tf  variables_iam.tf  outputs_iam.tf ← iam (always)
├── ecr.tf  deploy_policy_ecr.tf  outputs_ecr.tf
├── ecs.tf  iam_ecs.tf  deploy_policy_ecs.tf  variables_ecs.tf  outputs_ecs.tf
├── db_local.tf                              ← from db_local.empty.tf  (= var.database_url)
└── terraform.tfvars.example                 ← includes  database_url = "CHANGE_ME"
```

**full infra** (or `--only ecs rds`; rds **present** → when-rds branch):
```
infra/
├── main.tf  variables.tf  .gitignore        ← _core
├── iam.tf  variables_iam.tf  outputs_iam.tf ← iam (always)
├── ecr.tf  deploy_policy_ecr.tf  outputs_ecr.tf
├── database.tf  variables_rds.tf  outputs_rds.tf
├── storage.tf  outputs_s3.tf
├── ecs.tf  iam_ecs.tf  deploy_policy_ecs.tf  variables_ecs.tf  outputs_ecs.tf
├── db_local.tf                              ← from db_local.when-rds.tf  (= live RDS endpoint)
└── terraform.tfvars.example                 ← NO database_url line (it's computed)
```

Note what's gone in the output: no `.when-rds`/`.empty` infixes, no `*.tfvars.fragment` files (they're concatenated into `terraform.tfvars.example`), and only one `db_local.tf`. Terraform then auto-merges all the flat `*.tf` into one module.

content.text:
Good question to pin down. Short answer: **`when-rds.tf` yes, `empty.tf` yes (can't drop it), and the fragment is the only one that's truly optional.** Here's why the empty `.tf` can't collapse into the fragment.

## The crux: a `.tf` *declares*, a fragment *assigns*

`ecs.tf` has this one line:

```hcl
value = local.database_url
```

So `local.database_url` **must be defined in every ecs scaffold**, or `terraform validate` fails with "reference to undeclared local." Two different definitions, mutually exclusive:

- rds present → `db_local.when-rds.tf`: `local.database_url = "<live RDS ref>"`
- rds absent → `db_local.empty.tf`: declares `variable "database_url"` **and** `local.database_url = var.database_url`

Now look at what the fragment actually is:

```hcl
# db_local.empty.tfvars.fragment  →  ends up in terraform.tfvars.example
database_url = "CHANGE_ME"
```

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\franc\.claude\skills\git-push

# git-push

Safely commit and push the current changes. Every run follows this exact sequence:

## 1. Safety check

Run `git status` to see what will be staged. Review the actual file list for:

- **Secrets** — `.env`, `.pem`, `.key`, credentials, tokens, API keys
- **Internal data** — data dumps, migration exports, board exports, JSON/CSV with names/tasks/internal info, database exports. Any folder that looks like a one-off dump (e.g. `*-migration/`, `*-export/`, `*-dump/`) is a red flag.
- **Large binaries** — blobs, images, compiled files that don't belong in git
- **Files that should be gitignored** — check if the repo is public, and whether the file contains anything that shouldn't be on GitHub
- **Local filesystem paths** — grep staged text files (README, docs, configs, examples) for absolute local paths: `C:\Users\...`, `C:/Francisco/...`, `/Users/<name>/...`, `/home/<name>/...`, `/mnt/c/...`, `~/<name>/...`. These leak the author's machine layout and username. Also watch for hardcoded local hostnames, LAN IPs (`192.168.*`, `10.*`), and `localhost:<port>` references that only make sense on the author's box.

Local paths are a **fixable cosmetic leak**, not a blocker. When you find one:

1. Replace it with a generic placeholder (`/path/to/repo`, `<repo-root>`, `~/projects/<repo>`) or a repo-relative path.
2. If the path is inside an example command, keep the command runnable — use a clearly-placeholder token like `<your-username>` so readers know to substitute.
3. Re-stage the edited file before committing. Do NOT ask the user for permission to scrub a local path — just fix it and mention it in the heads-up.

Only stop if you find a **real problem** (secrets, dumps, binaries). Do NOT theorize about what .gitignore *could* be missing — check the actual files. If every file in the diff is safe, move on silently.

## 2. Initialize git if missing

If `.git/` does not exist, run `git init` and continue. If it exists, skip.

## 3. Stage everything

```bash
git add .
```

## 4. Write the commit message

Use **conventional commits**. No co-authoring.

Every message MUST answer both **what** changed and **why** it changed.

- `feat:` for new functionality
- `fix:` for bug fixes
- `chore:` for everything else

Bad: `feat: add repo mapping` — missing the why.
Good: `feat: add repo mapping to centralize project navigation`

Bad: `fix: update query logic` — what query? why?
Good: `fix: deduplicate subsidiary query to avoid double-counting schedules`

Bad: `chore: update dependencies` — why now?
Good: `chore: bump django to 4.2.9 to patch CVE-2024-XXXXX`

Before writing the message, inspect both:

- the staged diff
- the current chat context / recent user requests

Check whether the staged work represents **one logical change** or **multiple logical changes bundled together** because everything was staged with `git add .`.

If the diff includes multiple distinct tasks or features, the commit message must say so explicitly instead of pretending everything is one small change. In that case:

- write a multi-line conventional commit message
- use one `type:` line per logical change
- make each line include both **what** changed and **why**
- order the lines by importance, with the main user-facing change first

Bad multi-change message:
`feat: update spotify playback`

Good multi-change message:
`feat: return playlist context in spotify playback responses to show what started playing
feat: add Droid MCP and skill deployment guidance to document the new local setup`

Another good multi-change message:
`feat: deploy personal skills to Droid to keep Claude and Droid installs in sync
docs: update skill guidelines to point at deploy_skills.py and Droid skill folders`

Do NOT invent a fake single-feature message when the diff clearly contains unrelated or semi-related work. The message should reflect the true scope of the commit.

Read the diff to understand the changes, then write the message. Use a HEREDOC:

```bash
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
type: what changed and why
EOF
)"
```

If there is nothing to commit yet (empty repo), create an initial commit after staging so step 5's `gh repo create --push` has something to push.

## 5. Ensure a GitHub remote exists

Run `git remote -v`. Three cases:

**a) A remote is already set** → skip to step 6.

**b) No remote at all** → create one on GitHub using `gh`:

1. Verify auth: `gh auth status`. If not logged in, stop and ask the user to run `gh auth login`.
2. Pick a repo name. Default: the current directory's basename. Confirm with the user before creating.
3. Default to **private** unless the user explicitly says public. Creating a public repo without asking is a mistake — code can contain secrets, half-finished work, or internal context the user didn't mean to publish.
4. Create and push in one call:

   ```bash
   gh repo create <name> --source=. --private --push
   ```

   This creates the GitHub repo, wires up `origin`, and pushes the current branch with upstream tracking. Do not run `git push` again afterward.

**c) Remote exists but the current branch has no upstream** → push with `-u`:

```bash
git push -u origin <current-branch>
```

## 6. Push

If step 5 already pushed (cases b and c), skip this step. Otherwise:

```bash
git push
```

**Read the push output.** If GitHub has renamed or transferred the repo, it prints something like:

```
remote: This repository moved. Please use the new location:
remote:   https://github.com/<org>/<new-name>.git
```

The push still succeeds via redirect, but the local `origin` still points at the old name. When you see this notice, update the URL on the spot:

```bash
git remote set-url origin https://github.com/<org>/<new-name>.git
```

Use the exact URL printed after "new location:". Tell the user you updated the origin URL and show the new value.

## Rules

- NEVER skip any step.
- NEVER push if the audit flagged something — resolve it first.
- NEVER add a Co-Authored-By line.
- NEVER create a public repo without explicit user consent. Default to private.
- NEVER guess the repo name — confirm with the user before `gh repo create`.
- If there are no changes to commit and the remote is already up to date, say so and stop.
- If a pre-commit hook fails, fix the issue and create a NEW commit (don't amend).
